bet.dominantBottleneck: The dominant bottleneck is controlling semiconductor surface behavior and doping/junction formation well enough to make transistor fabrication reproducible and yield-determined, converting a demonstrated effect into a manufacturable electronics platform rather than a laboratory curiosity.

routes.route: Systematic surface-stabilization program: chemically and physically characterize and passivate germanium/silicon surfaces to reduce contamination-driven variability and drift.
routes.reason: Surface effects are identified as material, and stabilizing them is a prerequisite for any reproducible device; high-information, low-cost experiments on surface chemistry directly attack the stated variability bottleneck.

routes.route: Junction-transistor route via controlled doping and junction formation in high-purity germanium/silicon, emphasizing alloys and grown junctions over point contact.
routes.reason: Junction devices are theorized as more robust than point-contact; improving purification and controlled junctions yields better uniformity and is a direct step toward a platform rather than a single fragile device.

routes.route: Photographic-mask and localized diffusion/deposition experiments to test whether batch-style fabrication of multiple devices on one substrate is physically plausible.
routes.reason: Masking and localized processing are the kernel of integrated fabrication; testing them at laboratory scale gives early information on whether monolithic concepts can ever repay their added complexity, without assuming a solved planar process.

routes.route: Discrete and hybrid assembly optimization: assemble packaged discrete transistors into circuits and measure yield, wiring failure, and reliability to quantify the system-level burden.
routes.reason: The constraints emphasize that interconnection and reliability matter as much as single-device performance; quantitative data on discrete-assembly failure rates are needed to judge whether monolithic fabrication is worth its added complexity.

routes.route: Monolithic fabrication-concept feasibility studies that fabricate and characterize a few co-processed devices on one substrate to probe isolation, cross-talk, and yield trade-offs explicitly.
routes.reason: Without a resolved planar silicon process and stable surfaces, committing major resources to full monolithic circuits risks premature investment; limited feasibility studies keep the option alive while cheaper routes mature first.

bet.dominantBottleneck: The dominant bottleneck is reproducibility and yield: the transistor effect works in isolated demonstrations, but device-to-device variation, surface contamination instability, and the absence of any proven batch fabrication platform prevent the effect from becoming a dependable electronic-system building block. Wiring and packaging hundreds of individually made, varied devices creates reliability and cost barriers that dwarf single-device performance.

routes.route: Develop a diffusion-based junction transistor process with controlled doping profiles and measure yield statistics across batches to establish a reproducible base device.
routes.reason: High-purity germanium/silicon and controlled doping are available; junction theory already points to more robust structures than point contacts. Yield measurement is the cheapest way to learn whether reproducibility is achievable before any integration attempt.

routes.route: Attack surface contamination and passivation directly with chemical treatments and surface-state measurements, since surface instability is a known and unresolved failure source for all junction devices.
routes.reason: Surface effects materially change behavior per the evidence packet; without solving surface stability every downstream fabrication and packaging approach inherits this failure. This is a discriminating test of whether junction devices can be field-reliable at all.

routes.route: Optimize discrete monolithic fabrication of a few interconnected devices (e.g., a two-transistor circuit) on one chip using photographic masks and local diffusion, to test whether multi-device monolithic integration is physically viable.
routes.reason: Masking and localized diffusion are plausible lab techniques; proving even two or three working interconnected devices on one crystal tests the integration premise cheaply, before assuming a full planar platform.

routes.route: Pursue hybrid packaging where separately made and pre-tested discrete junction devices are mounted on a common substrate with printed/welded interconnects, trading assembly burden for component-level screening.
routes.reason: Given current yield variation, pre-screening individual devices before assembly can partially compensate for lack of reproducibility and offers near-term system reliability even if monolithic integration fails.

routes.route: Investigate alloy-junction transistor fabrication as an alternative to diffusion, exploiting the melting/junction-forming behavior of doped materials to get better control with simpler processing.
routes.reason: Alloy junctions may offer easier junction formation than diffusion early on, but diffusion aligns better with eventual masked batch integration; the decision can wait until diffusion yield data shows whether a simpler route is needed.

routes.route: Build a comparison of reliability and system cost between a discrete-transistor system, a hybrid system, and a small monolithic multi-device chip to give buyers quantitative tradeoff data.
routes.reason: The upgrade criterion is yield/reliability/system cost, and military/space buyers tolerate high cost for size and reliability; knowing these numbers decides which fabrication complexity repays itself.

bet.dominantBottleneck: The dominant bottleneck is converting a demonstrated but fragile point-contact/junction transistor effect into a reproducible, manufacturable electronics platform: device-to-device variation, surface instability, and the wiring/reliability burden of discrete assemblies all converge on the absence of a proven batch process for fabricating and interconnecting complete circuits at scale.

routes.route: Develop a localized diffusion/deposition mesafabrication route using photographic masks to define and protect junctions on high-purity germanium, then assemble discrete mesa transistors into hybrid subassemblies to build reliability data.
routes.reason: Masking plus controlled diffusion is a plausible contemporaneous route; building hybrid assemblies from improved mesa devices directly attacks the yield/reliability bottleneck and generates discriminating data without assuming a solved monolithic platform.

routes.route: Focus on surface-stabilization science: chemically passivate and encapsulate germanium/silicon surfaces, measure channel-effect stability and leakage over time, and identify reproducible surface treatments.
routes.reason: Surface contamination is explicitly unresolved and materially changes device behavior; a stable passivation method is a necessary complement to any fabrication route and can be tested with ordinary chemistry labs and curve-tracer characterization.

routes.route: Pursue a monolithic integration concept at laboratory scale: pattern a full circuit (resistors, capacitors, transistors) on one semiconductor slice using masks and sequential diffusions, accepting low initial yield.
routes.reason: The pressure explicitly targets a systems platform, and military/space buyers tolerate high early cost for size/reliability; a low-yield lab-scale monolithic demonstrator gives the highest-information answer to whether the concept can ever repay its complexity.

routes.route: Optimize alloyed/ grown-junction discrete transistors as an incremental improvement to current point-contact and early junction devices, quantifying parameter spread and drift distributions under stress.
routes.reason: Improving the discrete device alone does not resolve the interconnection and assembly bottleneck that dominates system cost/reliability, though its characterization data is useful; defer pending results from mesafabrication and surface passivation work.

routes.route: Advance germanium purification and crystal-growth control to reduce defect density and improve doping uniformity across slices.
routes.reason: High-purity material is difficult but improving, and material uniformity underpins every fabrication route; improving bulk material quality raises the ceiling on all route outcomes at modest cost.

routes.route: Develop standardized hybrid packaging that minimizes internal wiring: printed-wiring substrates, face-down or flip-chip-like attachment of discrete/hybrid devices, and sealed encapsulation to protect against contamination.
routes.reason: Interconnections dominate failure modes; a near-term packaging/hybrid discipline addresses the most concrete reliability problem while monolithic alternatives mature, and it is construable from photographic-mask and assembly capabilities available now.

bet.dominantBottleneck: The dominant bottleneck is scaling complete viral inactivation and antigenic potency from a single validated trial formulation to millions of independently manufactured industrial lots, where the field trial demonstrated population-level protection but did not test the full production system under scale, diverse manufacturers, and lot-to-lot variability. Mass production turns rare residual-live-virus events into many-recipient exposures, while potency retention and inactivation completeness pull process control in opposite directions. Trial efficacy and factory reproducibility are distinct evidence sources, and the current lot-testing regime has not yet been stress-tested by a mass campaign.

routes.route: Tighten production controls and lot-release sampling/verification, treating each independently manufactured lot as a mini-trial subject to inactivation-kinetics and potency acceptance criteria before release.
routes.reason: This directly addresses the factory-reproducibility gap using capabilities we already hold (holding/rejecting lots, tightening sampling/verification) and is the highest-information route for controlling the residual-live-virus risk at scale.

routes.route: Conduct post-vaccination disease surveillance and epidemiologic investigation in parallel with rollout, distinguishing background polio from vaccine-associated cases to catch rare failures before they cascade.
routes.reason: Surveillance is available now and provides the early-warning safety net; it also generates population-scale evidence that the lot tests alone cannot, though it cannot precede release and so is a complement, not the decisive test.

routes.route: Continue research/trials on the live-attenuated oral vaccine candidate as an independent parallel program, without assuming its later success or premature deployment.
routes.reason: The OPV route remains the only serious alternative path and hedges against a hidden mass-scale inactivation failure; but it lacks domestic licensure and deployment status at cutoff, so it should be pursued as a parallel hedge, not as the primary near-term intervention.

routes.route: Manufacture inactivated-virus vaccine using only existing licensed process steps, adding potency-versus-inactivation stress testing across worst-case production batches before mass release.

routes.route: Rigorous pre-licensure lot-release verification: tighten inactivation/potency per-lot testing, require independent verification of each manufacturer's first production runs before broad release, and stage deployment by lot and region.
routes.reason: The trial validates the formulation; the remaining uncertainty is per-lot safety and potency. Staged release with stringent lot testing gives the highest-information path to scale while limiting worst-case exposure if any single lot fails.

routes.route: Rapid mass production with parallel lot testing under time pressure to meet intense public demand, accepting that surveillance will catch problems after-the-fact.
routes.reason: A rare manufacturing failure can affect many recipients at scale, and potency vs. complete inactivation pulls process control in opposing directions; post-hoc surveillance is too slow and too insensitive to background disease to serve as the primary safety net for the full system.

routes.route: Invest in process-control improvements independent of lot testing: tighter raw-material specs, validated inactivation kinetics, standardized reactor/incubation parameters across manufacturers, and reproducibility runs before licensure.
routes.reason: Lot testing detects failures but does not prevent them; tightening process control across the many independent manufacturers is the complement that makes each lot more likely to pass tests and reduces the probability of a rare failure at scale.

routes.route: Defer mass manufacture until the competing live-attenuated oral candidate matures and provides an alternative or combined domestic deployment.
routes.reason: The oral route is early in research and lacks domestic licensure/deployment status at this cutoff; deferring an effective injected intervention on this basis has real disease cost and no high-information near-term payoff, so it should be revisited only as the oral program's outcomes resolve.

routes.route: Build population-level vaccine-associated paralysis surveillance to separate background disease from vaccine-associated cases during the campaign, feeding data back into lot-hold decisions.
routes.reason: Public-health surveillance must distinguish background disease from vaccine-associated cases; this is an ongoing evidence stream that sharpens lot-hold thresholds and lets regulators tighten or release lots based on real-world signal.

routes.route: Accelerate animal and in-vitro safety data for each lot beyond the then-current tests, seeking more sensitive markers of residual live virus, before releasing each lot to the public.
routes.reason: Adding unvalidated, not-yet-sensitive tests to the lot-release workflow could delay millions of doses without proven incremental safety value; effort is better spent on validated inactivation + process control now, while keeping research open on better residual-virus assays.

routes.route: Tighten production controls and lot-release sampling/verification for the inactivated vaccine, emphasizing per-batch inactivation titers to guarantee complete kill while guarding potency by controlled antigen-dose windows.
routes.reason: This directly attacks the dominant bottleneck of factory reproducibility; the trial proved the formulation works, so manufacturing consistency and residual-live-virus assurance are the cheapest high-information next tests.

routes.route: Hold/reject vaccine lots based on process/test evidence rather than relying only on final product potency, building an in-process inactivation kill-curve database across multiple plants.
routes.reason: Independent verification distributed across manufacturers provides the first discriminating evidence on whether the 'complete inactivation + retained potency' process is robust or operator-dependent before mass release.

routes.route: Post-vaccination disease surveillance and epidemiologic investigation designed to distinguish background paralysis from possible vaccine-associated cases and to detect any rare breakthrough at scale.
routes.reason: Surveillance is the only way the field learns a rare manufacturing failure at scale in real time; it is a cheap complement that runs in parallel with manufacture, though it cannot substitute for upstream process control.

routes.reason: The oral route is a serious rival that could offer easier administration and mucosal immunity, and it is an unresolved unknown; keeping it alive preserves options if the inactivated manufacturing scale-up proves brittle.

routes.route: Run a pilot multi-plant industrial-scale lot production campaign (not a new efficacy trial) before full national deployment, using tightened controls and holding lots until combined process/test evidence clears them.
routes.reason: This is the highest-information discriminating test of the true bottleneck: it tests whether the full production system, not a single trial plant, can reproducibly meet inactivation/potency windows under industrial conditions.

bet.dominantBottleneck: Launch mass and rendezvous/docking reliability: no single Saturn-class launcher can lift the direct-ascent round-trip mass, so the architecture must split the payload across launches and validate orbital rendezvous (in Earth and later lunar orbit) on a hard schedule, all while preserving abort/recovery paths and preventing a new docking dependence from outweighing the mass savings.

routes.route: Lunar-orbit-rendezvous (LOR): keep command/service module in lunar orbit while a lighter lander descends; requires a lunar-orbit rendezvous, which has never been done under crewed conditions.
routes.reason: Largest whole-system mass reduction (only a small module lands and re-ascends); directly addresses the hard launch-mass constraint; available capability to develop rendezvous/docking and guidance can be staged first in Earth orbit.

routes.route: Earth-orbit-rendezvous (EOR): assemble and refuel the full translunar stack in low Earth orbit from multiple Saturn launches; no lunar rendezvous needed but adds orbital assembly and propellant-transfer complexity.
routes.reason: Spreads launch burden across the Saturn family without demanding lunar rendezvous, but orbital assembly and cryogenic transfer are immature and add whole-system risk; keep as fallback if lunar rendezvous proves unreliable in Earth-orbit tests.

routes.route: Direct ascent with single heavy launcher: one vehicle carries everything to the lunar surface and back, maximizing schedule simplicity in mission design but requiring the largest Saturn growth variant and heaviest payload.
routes.reason: The manifest explicitly records that existing launchers cannot fly a direct round trip at required mass; pushing to a single mega-launcher stretches Saturn-family schedule and mass far beyond what is credible before the deadline.

routes.route: Hybrid EOR-plus-LOR: assemble in Earth orbit but still split the lunar stack so only the lander descends, combining assembly with a lunar rendezvous.
routes.reason: Adds both orbital-assembly complexity and lunar rendezvous; higher integration risk than LOR alone and only marginally better mass margin; revisit only if LOR mass budget fails.

routes.route: Unmanned precursor landings (Surveyor/robotic probes plus an unpiloted lunar-orbit rendezvous rehearsal) to validate guidance, braking, landing and docking before crew commitment.
routes.reason: Directly uses the staged precursor and test-failure-revision capability; highest-information, lowest-cost de-risking of the two risky links (lunar landing and lunar rendezvous) before committing crews.
